blocks.text: **The problem.** A sorted array of **distinct** values has been **rotated**: some number of values were moved from the front to the back, so `[0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7]` might become `[4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]`. Given the rotated array, return its **minimum** value in **O(log n)** time.

blocks.alt: The rotated array 4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2 is two sorted runs: 4 to 7, then 0 to 2. Every value in the first run is bigger than the last value, 2; every value in the second run is at most 2. Asking 'is nums[i] at most the last value?' gives no, no, no, no, yes, yes, yes, and the first yes, index 4, is the minimum.

nums = [3, 4, 5, 1, 2]           ->  1

nums = [11, 13, 15, 17]          ->  11   (rotated all the way round: sorted again)

blocks.text: A rotated sorted array is **two sorted runs** glued together, the second run made of smaller values. It isn't sorted, but it keeps enough order for binary search: at any `mid`, at least one side of it is a sorted run, and a single comparison tells you which. The three problems in this chapter all start from that fact — find the seam, search a value, then cope with duplicates that hide the seam.
The idea: compare mid with the last value

Every value in the first run is **bigger** than the array's last value, and every value in the second run is **at most** it. So `nums[mid] > nums[high]` means mid is in the first run and the minimum — the start of the second run — is to its right: `low = mid + 1`. Otherwise mid is in the second run, and the minimum is mid or to its left: `high = mid`. Comparing with `nums[high]` (not `nums[low]`) also handles an array that isn't rotated at all.

def find_min(nums):
    return min(nums)                      # a linear scan

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(1).** It ignores the structure entirely.

blocks.caption: Compare mid with the last value of the range to see which run mid is in.

blocks.text: **Time O(log n), space O(1).** The index `low` it stops at is also the **rotation count**: how many places the sorted array was rotated.

rows.timeWhy: It checks **every value** for the smallest.
Comparing `mid` with the **last value** tells which half holds the seam: the range halves each step.

items: **Not rotated** (or rotated n times) — `[11, 13, 15, 17]`: the first value.
